newsitem.title: UK: Competition in UK power generation inadequate -MPs.
newsitem.headline: Competition in UK power generation inadequate -MPs.

text.p: Competition in Britain's electricity generation industry is increasing but is not yet adequate, parliament's trade and industry committee said on Tuesday.

In a report on energy regulation, the all-party committee recommended that Stephen Littlechild, the director general of electricty supply, consider adopting further measures to accelerate the development of effective competition.
"The possibility of the further sale of capacity by the two main generators should not be excluded," the committee said.
The MPs were pleased to note that the price-setting influence of National Power Plc and Powergen Plc was declining.
"But we are not yet convinced that sufficiently robust competition exists to guarantee that consumers will obtain the best possible prices," the committee said.
The panel sidestepped the main opposition Labour party's controversial plan to levy a windfall tax on the excess profits of privatised utilities.
"No details have been made available to us, and we have not inquired into the matter," its report said.

However, in a conclusion likely to be seized upon by Labour as justifying the windfall tax, the MPs concluded that the figures for X in the RPI-X price control formula were set too low in order to make energy company flotations attractive.

"Both energy regulators believe the net result was that the initial price controls unduly favoured shareholders over customers. We agree, though we find it hard to see how it would have been possible prior to flotation to have accurately estimated likely efficiency gains," the report said.

Moreover, it said the regulators had set progressively more stringent price controls as they had become more experienced with the system, partly redressing the balance between shareholders and consumers.
The MPs recommended that the RPI-X formula of regulation should be continued.

Although further work needs to be done to improve the estimation of X, the form has much to commend it over other methods, above all because it provides powerful incentives to companies to reduce costs by improving efficiency.
"We recognise that profit-sharing has not been sufficiently developed or tested and we do not rule it out as an option for the future," the MPs added.

-- Information relating to natural monopolies should be assumed to be non-confidential, unless it can be shown to be otherwise, and the gas and electricity regulators should be given the authority to publish it as they see fit.
-- When competition in supply is fully established in the gas and electricity industries, the government should reconsider whether it is necessary to have separate regulators for the two sectors.
